Newborn Care

Umbilical Cord Care and Common Newborn Skin Issues

Updated: July 1, 2026

Newborn skin does a lot of strange and completely normal things in the first weeks — and the umbilical cord stump, while odd-looking, mostly just needs to be left alone. Here is what is normal, what needs simple care, and what deserves a call to the doctor.

Caring for the cord stump

The golden rule of cord care is "keep it clean and dry, and let it be." The stump typically dries, darkens, and falls off on its own within one to three weeks. Modern guidance in most places is dry care — no alcohol or ointments unless your provider specifically advises them.

Fold the diaper down below the stump so urine does not soak it, stick to sponge baths until it falls off, and never pull at it — even when it is hanging by a thread. It will let go when it is ready.

Signs of cord infection

A little dried blood or slight crustiness as the stump separates is normal. What is not: redness spreading on the skin around the base, swelling, a foul smell, yellow discharge or pus, or a baby who cries when the area is touched.

Contact your pediatrician promptly if you see those signs, or if your baby also has a fever or seems unusually unwell. Cord infections are uncommon but need quick attention.

Peeling, blotchy, brand-new skin

After months in fluid, newborn skin often peels and flakes in the first weeks — especially on hands, feet, and ankles. It needs no treatment, though a plain, fragrance-free baby moisturizer is fine if you want to use one.

Blotchy patches, temporary color changes, and the scattered red spots of erythema toxicum (a harmless, common newborn rash) also come and go on their own. Newborn skin is a moving target that settles with time.

Baby acne and milia

Baby acne — small red or white bumps on the cheeks, nose, and forehead — often appears in the first weeks and clears on its own within weeks to a few months. Wash with plain water, skip scrubbing, and resist all creams unless your provider suggests one.

Milia are tiny white pearls on the nose and face caused by blocked pores. They are extremely common, painless, and vanish by themselves. No squeezing — truly, none.

Cradle cap

Cradle cap shows up as greasy, yellowish, scaly patches on the scalp (sometimes eyebrows too). It is common, harmless, and not itchy or bothersome to the baby.

If you want to loosen it, massage a little plain baby oil or petroleum jelly into the scalp, let it sit, then brush gently with a soft baby brush and shampoo. It usually resolves over weeks to months either way.

When to ask the doctor

Call your provider about any rash that comes with fever, blisters or fluid-filled spots, a very unwell or unusually sleepy baby, or a rash that is spreading fast or looks angry rather than mild.

And when in doubt, just ask — pediatricians look at newborn skin all day, and a quick photo or visit settles most worries in minutes. No question about a newborn is too small.

Key takeaways

  • Cord care is simple: keep the stump clean and dry, fold diapers below it, never pull it.
  • Spreading redness, swelling, pus, or foul smell at the cord means call the doctor promptly.
  • Peeling skin, blotches, and newborn rashes are usually normal and self-resolving.
  • Baby acne and milia clear on their own — no creams or squeezing needed.
  • Cradle cap is harmless; oil, gentle brushing, and patience are all it takes.

Frequently asked questions

When does the umbilical cord stump fall off?

Usually within one to three weeks. Let it detach on its own — pulling at it, even when it is barely attached, can cause bleeding or irritation.

Should I put alcohol on the cord stump?

Most current guidance recommends dry care — just keep the area clean and dry. Only use alcohol or other products if your own provider specifically advises it.

Is baby acne caused by something I ate or used?

No. Baby acne is thought to relate to normal newborn hormone shifts, not your diet or products. It clears on its own — plain water washing is all it needs.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
